case_study_insert.main_stem: Trailpine Freight (TPF) is a private limited company in the road freight and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2011 by Nelia Brooks, it operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. TPF plans to invest $480,000 in an electric delivery truck fleet and depot charging hub, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and $180,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and produces 45,000 units a year. TPF faces a rising consignment damage rate of 3.2% and driver absenteeism of 7%, which are slowing depot turnaround and worrying retail clients. The founder still chairs the board and sets delivery targets personally.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2025: TPF handled 45,000 consignments last year, up 6% on the previous year, with a consignment damage rate of 3.2% and 24 written customer complaints last month. On-time delivery stands at 91%, against a 97% target, and average depot turnaround is 38 minutes. A survey of 250 business clients found 68% would pay $0.60 more for guaranteed next-day delivery, and 54% choose carriers on environmental performance. Eleven of the 40 drivers still need electric-vehicle training, and the accredited course costs $700 per driver.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Trailpine Freight (TPF) for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, lifting borrowing costs on variable-rate business loans. (2) Diesel and depot electricity prices have risen 11.3% year-on-year, pushing up per-consignment operating costs. (3) The national minimum wage will rise 5.8% from $12.40 to $13.11 per hour from April 2026, increasing wage bills across the logistics sector.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for TPF of funding the $480,000 electric fleet from retained profit rather than the $300,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment obligation, so TPF keeps the cash needed to run 45,000 consignments a year. The base rate has moved from 4.5% to 5.25%, making the $300,000 five-year bank loan more expensive, whereas the $180,000 retained profit is free. With a $14.00 selling price and an $8.00 variable cost, every consignment earns $6.00 contribution, or $270,000 a year at current volume, and that cash can absorb the 11.3% rise in diesel and depot electricity without pushing the $14.00 price up to business clients.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids collateral and repossession risk on the $480,000 truck fleet and charging hub. If the 3.2% damage rate and 7% driver absenteeism delay the return from the new vehicles, no lender can seize the trucks or impose conditions on Nelia Brooks's delivery targets. Ownership and control stay with the founder, which suits a private limited company that wants to reinvest surplus in further depot capacity once the electric fleet is working.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to Trailpine Freight (TPF), its fleet investment and its cost structure.

questions.question_text: Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or targeted social-media advertising to business clients. Which should TPF choose to promote its next-day delivery service? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: A national TV campaign would build brand awareness quickly for TPF's next-day service and could reach the retail clients that receive its consignments. However, airtime and production are very expensive for a 40-employee private limited company funding a $480,000 electric fleet, and most viewers are not business buyers of road freight, so much of the spend would be wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is much cheaper and suits a time-limited message about a new depot service. It reaches listeners near TPF's hub, but the survey identifies buyers of logistics services rather than local listeners, and region-only coverage cannot help TPF fill the 45,000 consignments a year needed to cover $180,000 of fixed costs.

Targeted social-media advertising: Advertising on professional and industry platforms lets TPF aim at logistics and purchasing managers, the same kind of respondents as the 250 business clients surveyed. It is measurable, far cheaper than television, and can demonstrate the 91% on-time delivery record and the guaranteed next-day service bought by the 68% who would pay $0.60 more. Its weakness is slower mass-brand recognition than television.

Recommendation: TPF should choose targeted social-media advertising. It reaches the decision-makers in the survey, costs a fraction of television, and supports the $0.60 premium that protects the $6.00 contribution ($14.00 − $8.00). National television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a business servicing a $300,000 loan; local radio is rejected as too narrow and aimed at consumers rather than business freight buyers. TPF can measure enquiries against the 250-client survey before committing further spend.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with minimal application to TPF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TPF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in the context of TPF with a justified recommendation explaining why national television and local radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for TPF of using democratic leadership to reduce its 7% driver absenteeism and 3.2% consignment damage rate.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the 40 drivers help plan routes and charging schedules, giving them a voice in how the electric fleet is introduced. Higher involvement raises job satisfaction and commitment, so the 7% absenteeism rate should fall. That matters because every missing driver slows depot turnaround beyond the current 38 minutes and puts the 45,000-consignment plan at risk; each consignment lost represents $6.00 of contribution ($14.00 − $8.00).

Point 2: Drivers who handle consignments daily can suggest practical fixes for the 3.2% damage rate, such as better loading routines, which a distant manager might miss. Involvement also builds ownership of quality, helping cut the 24 written complaints and protect the 91% on-time delivery record. Better retention reduces reliance on the $700 electric-vehicle training course for replacement drivers, while Nelia Brooks keeps final authority over delivery targets. Nelia Brooks can reinforce the message at the depot without adding to the $180,000 fixed-cost base.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual analysis linked to TPF's absenteeism, damage rate and depot performance.

questions.question_text: Consider quality circles in which drivers solve the 3.2% damage problem, or a cash bonus for damage-free deliveries. Which should TPF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Quality circles: Regular driver groups would examine why 3.2% of consignments are damaged and propose loading or routing improvements. This uses the knowledge of the 40 drivers, suits democratic leadership, and can lift on-time delivery from 91% toward the 97% target without adding a new payment. It is slow to produce results and needs management time, and some suggestions may conflict with the $480,000 fleet schedule.

Cash bonus: A payment for damage-free deliveries gives an immediate individual incentive and could quickly reduce the 24 written complaints. It rewards the right outcome and is easy to understand, but the insert gives no bonus rate or number of eligible drivers, so its total cost cannot be calculated. It may also encourage drivers to record damage inaccurately and does not fix underlying depot causes.

Decision: TPF should choose quality circles first, adding a bonus only if progress stalls. Quality circles address the cause of the 3.2% damage rate, fit the existing leadership style and cost nothing quantified in the insert, protecting the $6.00 contribution on 45,000 consignments. The cash bonus is rejected because its cost is unquantified and it treats symptoms rather than causes; TPF can introduce it later alongside the $700 training programme if the damage rate does not fall.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to TPF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of TPF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and uses TPF's figures.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TPF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($14.00 − $8.00) = $180,000 ÷ $6.00 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 consignments a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.00 − $8.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TPF's management can use this cost and break-even data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 30,000-unit break-even with actual output of 45,000 consignments: the margin of safety is 15,000 consignments, showing how far volume can fall before the electric-fleet investment stops covering $180,000 of fixed costs.
2. Use the $6.00 contribution to test the $0.60 price premium supported by 68% of surveyed clients: even a small discount from $14.00 can be modelled against the $8.00 variable cost before retail clients are offered a new deal.
3. Check that 45,000 consignments generating $6.00 each, or $270,000 of contribution, can service the $300,000 bank loan as the 5.25% base rate raises borrowing costs.
4. Benchmark unit cost: $180,000 ÷ 45,000 + $8.00 = $12.00 a consignment, a baseline for judging whether the 3.2% damage rate and 7% absenteeism are wasting depot capacity.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 15,000-unit margin of safety against $180,000 fixed costs; $0.60 premium and pricing modelling on the $14.00 price and $8.00 variable cost; $270,000 contribution to service the $300,000 loan; unit-cost benchmarking at $12.00 to tackle damage and absenteeism.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TPF's profitability between 2024 and 2025. Has profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 44.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 trading surplus after direct costs was $540,000 − $324,000 = $216,000; 2025 it was $630,000 − $352,800 = $277,200. Operating return against revenue: $54,000 ÷ $540,000 × 100 and $75,600 ÷ $630,000 × 100. Return against capital: $54,000 ÷ $360,000 × 100 and $75,600 ÷ $420,000 × 100. Revenue grew $90,000 while direct costs rose only $28,800, so more of each sales dollar survived to cover the $480,000 fleet programme.

Evaluation: All three measures moved in the same favourable direction. The trading surplus share of sales rose from 40.0% to 44.0%, suggesting better control of direct costs as consignment volume grew. The operating share of sales improved from 10.0% to 12.0%, showing that overheads did not grow as fast as revenue. Return on the capital base rose from 15.0% to 18.0% even though capital employed increased from $360,000 to $420,000, so the extra investment in trucks and charging is already being used productively. Interest payable fell from $9,000 to $8,000, helping operating profit, but the higher 5.25% base rate may reverse that benefit.

Conclusion: TPF's profitability has improved. The 40.0% to 44.0% trading margin, 10.0% to 12.0% operating margin and 15.0% to 18.0% return on capital all confirm the improvement, with the strongest evidence being the rise in return on capital because it shows the new fleet investment is earning more, not just that sales are higher.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements and a justified improved judgement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TPF of offering guaranteed next-day delivery to the business clients it surveyed.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 250 business clients found 68% would pay $0.60 more for guaranteed next-day delivery. If that premium is accepted, the $14.00 selling price can rise toward $14.60 while the $8.00 variable cost stays the same, raising contribution above the current $6.00 a consignment. It also reinforces the 91% on-time delivery record and helps TPF win business from clients who currently choose carriers on environmental performance.

Disadvantage: A guarantee creates a liability when the 3.2% damage rate or 7% driver absenteeism causes a missed delivery slot. The insert gives no refund or penalty figures, so the cost of failures cannot be quantified, but every failed consignment also risks the 24 complaints rising and weakens the premium offer. Meeting a tighter promise could require more depot resources than the $180,000 fixed-cost budget allows, so the net gain from the $0.60 premium cannot be assumed. TPF should monitor written complaints after launch to check that the premium is actually being earned.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to TPF's survey, service record and cost data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 11.3% rise in diesel and depot electricity prices and the 5.8% minimum wage rise to $13.11 will affect TPF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. If the $300,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.0075 × $300,000 = $2,250 a year. That is small beside $180,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the direct saving is zero. The higher rate may still make future finance for the $480,000 fleet dearer, but TPF can reduce this risk by fixing the loan rate.

Diesel and depot electricity prices (up 11.3%): This is a cost on every one of the 45,000 consignments. The insert gives a single $8.00 variable cost and does not decompose it, so only an upper bound is defensible: if the whole $8.00 rose 11.3%, that adds 0.113 × $8.00 = $0.90 a consignment, or about $40,680 a year (45,000 × $0.90). That would cut contribution from $6.00 toward $5.10 and threaten the $0.60 premium plan.

Minimum wage rise (5.8%, $12.40 to $13.11 an hour): The insert gives no hours worked or driver pay, so no annual wage total can be invented. The honest benchmark is productivity: 45,000 consignments ÷ 40 drivers = 1,125 consignments per driver, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or volume grows.

Conclusion: The 11.3% energy-price rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 45,000 consignments and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution that funds the fleet, unlike the conditional $2,250 interest effect and the wage rise, which cannot be quantified from the insert. TPF should revisit this judgement if the loan rate is later fixed, which would remove even the conditional interest effect.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to TPF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TPF's costs, contribution or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes using derivations shown from insert figures, with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement and reasons for rejecting the other two.
